slice: Yamaha YZ450F 2018-2022 generation; YZ450FX 2019-2026; WR250F and WR450F 2020-2026 (off-road differences, US restrictions, uncorking)

records.statement: The 2018-2022 YZ450F is the first electric-start, Wi-Fi-tunable generation of Yamaha's reversed-head 450: all-new for 2018, minor updates for 2019, a new cylinder head, brakes and frame details for 2020, then mostly carried over for 2021 and 2022 before the 2023 redesign.

source.name: Motocross Action, MXA race test: 2021 Yamaha YZ450F

records.notes: Assembled from Yamaha change lists as reported in the 2018 and 2021 race tests and Dirt Rider/Racer X model-year coverage.

records.statement: For 2018 Yamaha added electric start, a longer head pipe with lower head stays, a 29% larger airbox with one fastener, narrower radiator wings (about 1 in), and a smaller tank (1.9 to 1.6 gal).

source.name: Motocross Action, MXA race test: 2018 Yamaha YZ450F

records.notes: Cylinder angle change reported as 'tilted forward 2 degrees' in this source; see conflicts.

records.statement: The 2018 chassis sits lower and flatter: rear lowered 19 mm, trail up from 118 to 121 mm, swingarm pivot forging 10 mm wider, seat 8 mm lower in the middle and 19 mm lower at the rear, 22 mm offset clamps standard.

source.name: Motocross Action, MXA race test: 2018 Yamaha YZ450F

records.notes: Bars raised 5 mm on the 2018 mounts per the same source.

records.statement: For 2018 the clutch steel plates are ground on both sides and the pressure plate is stiffer; the fork damping cartridge grew from 24 to 25 mm and the shock spring went from 56 to 58 N/mm.

values.clutch: double-side ground steel plates, stiffer pressure plate

source.name: Motocross Action, MXA race test: 2018 Yamaha YZ450F

records.statement: 2018 was the first YZ450F tuned by phone over Wi-Fi: 16-cell fuel and ignition grids (the old handheld tuner had 9), with fuel in 2% steps and ignition in 1-degree steps; the older handheld GYTR Power Tuner does not work on it.

source.name: Motocross Action, MXA race test: 2018 Yamaha YZ450F

records.notes: Step sizes as reported by the magazine; another record (ypt-011) quotes about 3% per fuel step for the first app. See conflicts.

records.statement: 2019 was nearly a carryover: more contact area between the front wheel spacers and fork for front-end rigidity, slightly stiffer suspension, denser seat foam under the rider, and a 49-tooth rear sprocket instead of 48.

source.name: Dirt Bike, 2019 Yamaha YZ450F full test

records.notes: Seat-foam percentage from the 2021 race test (mxa21).

records.statement: For 2020 the head is 10 mm shorter with a steeper valve angle, the cams sit 14 mm closer together and 6 mm lower, compression rises to 13.0:1 with a new piston, the rod is 1.5 mm longer, and the head pipe is 3.2 mm larger in diameter.

source.name: Dirt Bike, 2020 Yamaha YZ450F full test

records.notes: New air filter and rectifier/capacitor unit also listed. Compression of 12.8:1 for 2018-2019 from mxa18c and dbt21fx.

records.statement: 2020 brought thinner inner frame-rail walls, revised engine mounts, a more flexible top clamp, bar mounts 5 mm lower (16.5 mm further forward than 2019), 10% stiffer seat foam, a front caliper piston up from 22.65 to 25.4 mm with 29.2% larger pads, and a rear disc down from 245 to 240 mm.

source.name: Motocross Action, MXA race test: 2021 Yamaha YZ450F

records.notes: Older rear wheels need the smaller rotor to fit (db20). Front axle inner-diameter change described inconsistently; see conflicts.

records.statement: The 2021 YZ450F had no engine, chassis or suspension changes, only new graphics and a Monster Energy edition; US prices were $9,399 standard and $9,599 Monster Energy.

source.name: Motocross Action, MXA race test: 2021 Yamaha YZ450F

records.notes: Racer X (rx21) also found no major 2021 changes.

records.statement: For 2022 the YZ450F got a lighter, thinner rear hub with cross-3 spoke lacing and new graphics at $9,599; sources disagree on whether suspension settings changed.

source.name: Dirt Bike Test, first look 2022 Yamaha four-stroke models

records.notes: One race test measured no real weight saving because the longer spokes offset the lighter hub (mxa22). See conflicts on suspension settings.

records.statement: On a magazine dyno the 2018 made 57.55 hp at 9,700 rpm versus 56.85 hp for the 2017, with 0.6 ft-lb less torque; the 2017 was slightly stronger from 5,000 to 8,000 rpm and the 2018 stronger from 8,000 to 11,000 rpm.

source.name: Motocross Action, MXA race test: 2018 Yamaha YZ450F

records.notes: Dyno brand not stated; stock map; repeated two days later with the same result. Yamaha had claimed +3 hp; not borne out.

records.statement: In a 2018 six-bike shootout the YZ450F made 52.3 hp at 9,900 rpm and 32.0 lb-ft at 7,800 rpm, fourth in power and tied last in torque.

source.name: Dirtbikes.com, 2018 450cc motocross shootout

records.notes: Rear-wheel dyno, brand not stated; fuel and map not stated. Despite the numbers, testers rated its engine best in class on the track.

records.statement: On an in-house Dynojet in third gear the 2019 made 50.09 hp at 9,650 rpm and 30.78 lb-ft at 7,510 rpm.

source.name: Cycle World / Dirt Rider, 2019 Yamaha YZ450F dyno

records.notes: Dynojet rear-wheel dyno, third gear; stock; fuel not stated. Also published at dirtrider.com/2019-yamaha-yz450f-dyno.

records.statement: On a magazine rear-wheel dyno the 2020 made 48.9 hp at 9,700 rpm and 29.3 lb-ft at 7,100 rpm, the lowest peak power and torque of the six 450s tested.

source.name: Dirt Rider, 2020 Yamaha YZ450F dyno test

records.notes: Rear-wheel dyno, brand not stated on the page (same outlet used a Dynojet 250i for other tests). Stock.

records.statement: A magazine dyno showed the 2020/2021 engine below the 2019 at every rpm, with its biggest gains from about 9,000 to 11,200 rpm; from 6,000 rpm to the high midrange it ranked near the bottom of the class and became competitive near 10,000 rpm.

source.name: Motocross Action, MXA race test: 2021 Yamaha YZ450F

records.notes: No absolute numbers published in the text; dyno brand not stated; 2021 engine identical to 2020.

records.statement: A magazine dyno gave the 2022 a class-leading 58.56 hp peak, reached about 500 rpm higher than the KTM or Honda, but it was fifth at 6,000 rpm, sixth at 7,000 rpm (almost 4 hp behind the CRF450) and ahead only of the KX450 at 8,000 rpm.

source.name: Motocross Action, MXA race test: 2022 Yamaha YZ450F

records.notes: Dyno brand, fuel and map not stated; stock. Do not compare with other outlets' numbers.

records.topic: test-rider map effect on the dyno (2018)
records.statement: A Yamaha test rider's map (TP map) added up to 2 hp in the midrange and up to 0.9 ft-lb of torque over the stock map, and moved peak power from 9,700 to 9,200 rpm.

source.name: Motocross Action, MXA race test: 2018 Yamaha YZ450F

records.notes: Testers found the stock 2018 map lean and flat down low; the three app maps did not help. Map is Yamaha's 'TP' preset (named after test rider Travis Preston). Grid values not in the article.

records.statement: The 2018 engine lost the 2017's dead spot between 6,000 and 7,000 rpm and its surge at 7,000, giving one long usable powerband; shootout riders called its throttle response the best in class and less abrupt than the 2017.

source.name: Motocross Action, MXA race test: 2018 Yamaha YZ450F

records.notes: Shootout feel from dbk18.

records.statement: Testers describe the 2019 as having massive low-end power and huge top end with the most linear delivery in the class, though it revs less quickly than the Honda or Kawasaki.

source.name: Dirt Bike, 2019 Yamaha YZ450F full test

records.notes: Test-rider (TP) map adds a sharper midrange hit.

records.statement: The 2020-2022 engine is smooth and linear with no flat spots but an abrupt, jerky first crack of throttle; below about 9,000 rpm it feels mellow, above 9,000 it does its best work, and engine braking is lighter so it coasts more into corners.

source.name: Motocross Action, MXA race test: 2021 Yamaha YZ450F

records.notes: Same picture in the 2022 race test (mxa22) and Dirt Bike 2020 (db20: smooth, no dead zones, no longer fastest on top). Dirt Rider 2022 (dbt22): jerky bottom in a low gear at high rpm, smoother mid-top. Yamaha's stated aim for the 2020 head/map was more controlled acceleration at small throttle openings (dr21fx).

records.statement: Testers credit the softer 2020-on character to the new head and a new standard map aimed at controlled small-throttle response; riding one gear high further softens the hit and engine braking and avoids stalling.

source.name: Dirt Bike, 2020 Yamaha YZ450F full test

records.notes: Gear-high tip repeated by dbt22 for experienced riders on the stock map.

records.statement: A magazine scale put the 2018 at 239 lb with electric start, 1 lb more than the 2017 and 17 lb more than the KTM 450 SX-F.

source.name: Motocross Action, MXA race test: 2018 Yamaha YZ450F

records.notes: Fuel condition not stated (this outlet usually weighs without fuel).

records.statement: A magazine scale put both the 2019 and 2020 at 239 lb without fuel.

source.name: Dirt Bike, 2020 Yamaha YZ450F full test

records.notes: 2019 figure from db19 (same outlet and scale).

records.statement: A magazine scale put the 2021 and 2022 at 238 lb, 15 lb more than a 223 lb KTM 450 SX-F.

source.name: Motocross Action, MXA race test: 2021 Yamaha YZ450F

records.notes: Same figure in mxa22.

records.statement: The 2018 turns in very accurately but feels loose on corner exit and twitchy at speed, with less straight-line stability than the KTM; on the 2019 riders who load the front hard on entry disliked the feedback while riders who back it in had no trouble.

source.name: Motocross Action, MXA race test: 2018 Yamaha YZ450F

records.notes: 2019 notes from db19. A later test called the 2018-2019 chassis very stable; see conflicts.

records.statement: From 2020 the chassis feels more precise, agile and lighter than the 2018-2019, still steered mainly with the rear; the lower, more forward bar position makes it easier to load the front wheel.

values.vs_2018_2019: more precise and agile, feels lighter

source.name: Dirt Bike Test, 2022 Yamaha YZ450F - same bike, new reputation

records.notes: db20: modest improvement, steer with rear. mxa21: handles better partly because of the mellower power.

records.statement: Testers' main gripe across this generation is ergonomics: bars too high and seat too low on the 2018-2019 (pushing the rider rearward), a firm, cupped seat that packs down, and a cramped cockpit for tall riders; a taller GYTR seat helps riders over 6 ft.

source.name: Motocross Action, MXA race test: 2021 Yamaha YZ450F

records.notes: 2018: testers went back to 2017 bar mounts (mxa18). 2019: bars high, seat low (db19). 2022: position 3 suits most but short riders found it a reach (dbt22).

records.statement: The 2018-2022 runs KYB SSS coil-spring forks with 5.0 N/mm springs and 290 cc oil, and a 58 N/mm shock spring with 100 mm stock race sag.

source.name: Motocross Action, MXA race test: 2021 Yamaha YZ450F

records.notes: Stock settings as listed in the race-test setup tables (mxa18, mxa21, mxa22). Fork compression: one click equals about two clicks of other brands' forks.

records.statement: Race-test setup for the 2018: fork compression 9 out (stock 8), rebound 8 out (stock 10), forks 5 mm up; shock 105 mm race sag, high-speed compression 1 turn out, low-speed 12 out, rebound 11 out.

source.name: Motocross Action, MXA race test: 2018 Yamaha YZ450F

records.notes: Stock springs; MX use.

records.statement: A 2019 test ran fork compression at 12 clicks out (8 stock), one click more rebound, and more than the recommended 100 mm sag; the previous year they used a taller seat and shorter bar pedestals.

source.name: Dirt Bike, 2019 Yamaha YZ450F full test

records.statement: A 2020 test found the fork worked for riders from about 150 lb to over 200 lb and ran about 105 mm of sag.

source.name: Dirt Bike, 2020 Yamaha YZ450F full test

records.statement: Race-test setup for the 2021: fork compression 9 out, rebound 8 out (stock 9), forks 5 mm up; shock 105 mm race sag, high-speed compression 1 turn out, low-speed 12 out, rebound 11 out; the 58 N/mm spring still gave usable sag for 130 lb riders.

source.name: Motocross Action, MXA race test: 2021 Yamaha YZ450F

records.notes: A 56 N/mm spring was carried for light riders but not needed.

records.statement: Race-test setup for the 2022: fork compression 11 out (stock 9), rebound 8 out (stock 9), forks 5 mm up; shock 105 mm race sag, high-speed compression 10 clicks out, low-speed 12 out, rebound 11 out.

source.name: Motocross Action, MXA race test: 2022 Yamaha YZ450F

records.notes: Shock high-speed listed in clicks in this year's table versus turns in 2018/2021.

records.topic: heavier riders: stiffer compression felt softer
records.statement: On the 2022, heavier testers found that adding compression made the bike feel softer because it rode higher and stopped reaching the stiff deep-stroke valving.

source.name: Dirt Bike Test, 2022 Yamaha YZ450F - same bike, new reputation

records.statement: A suspension shop lowered a 2018 for shorter riders with a 9 mm fork damper-rod limiter, a 0.110 in shock limiter and an adjustable pull rod at 143 mm (stock 142 mm), lowering the rear 13 mm in total; it turned better and the front felt less vague.

source.name: Motocross Action, problem-solving 2018 YZ450F build (Cycra/FTI)

records.notes: Valving left stock.

records.statement: A tuner build raised compression from 12.8:1 to 14.0:1 with a forged piston, added aftermarket valves and a full exhaust, and kept stock gearing because the extra low-mid power fixed the quick-revving second and sluggish third gear.

source.name: Motocross Action, problem-solving 2018 YZ450F build (Cycra/FTI)

records.notes: No dyno sheet published. Same build used an auto/torque-drive clutch with softer springs to reduce slip and lighten pull.

records.statement: Testers disliked the 2018's stock 48-tooth rear sprocket and preferred a 49 on tight and fast tracks; Yamaha fitted a 49 from 2019. Second, third and fourth gears are 1 mm wider for 2018 with unchanged ratios.

source.name: Motocross Action, MXA race test: 2018 Yamaha YZ450F

records.statement: Testers praised the 2018-2022 cable clutch as the best non-hydraulic clutch in the class with an easy pull; one off-road test got about 42 hours from the FX version before a precautionary change.

source.name: Motocross Action, MXA race test: 2021 Yamaha YZ450F

records.notes: Praise in mxa18, db19, db20, mxa21. 2022 race test listed the lack of a hydraulic clutch as a dislike, not a failure. Durability figure from dbt21fx (YZ450FX).

records.statement: The 2018 felt twitchy and loose at speed and on corner exit; testers fixed part of it by going back to the 2017 bar mounts and running forks 5 mm up, and Yamaha stiffened the front-wheel spacer contact for 2019 and lowered the bars for 2020.

source.name: Motocross Action, MXA race test: 2018 Yamaha YZ450F

records.notes: No source found describing a widespread head-shake failure on 2018-2019; see conflicts.

records.statement: The 2018's larger rotors on the old master cylinders and calipers gave weak initial bite and then grabbed; Yamaha redesigned both calipers for 2020.

source.name: Motocross Action, MXA race test: 2018 Yamaha YZ450F

records.statement: The flat foam filter sits on the backfire screen, dries out there and lets dirt through; testers use an aftermarket filter with a spacer or cage.

source.name: Motocross Action, MXA race test: 2021 Yamaha YZ450F

records.notes: Also flagged in mxa18 and mxa22. Same complaint on the 2023-2024 (yz45-068).

records.statement: Testers report sluggish hot restarts after a stall on the 2022 (not fixed by battery or map changes; a correct idle setting helps) and that the 2020 overheats quickly when idling.

source.name: Dirt Bike Test, 2022 Yamaha YZ450F - same bike, new reputation

records.notes: Overheating at idle from db20. Testers describe slow hot restart as common to the YZ four-stroke line.

records.statement: The wrap-around exhaust pipe is hard to remove, intake noise is loud, and fork compression clickers are hard to reach.

source.name: Motocross Action, MXA race test: 2022 Yamaha YZ450F

records.notes: Pipe removal also in mxa18; intake noise in db20.

records.statement: From 2020 riders can switch between two maps on the fly; the 2022 shipped with the same stock map in both switch positions, and testers usually loaded Yamaha's TP-3 preset to smooth low-throttle response (TP-5 and GC-1 also used).

source.name: Motocross Action, MXA race test: 2022 Yamaha YZ450F

records.notes: 2021 usage from mxa21. db20 preferred the new 2020 stock map over Yamaha's test map on loose, good-traction tracks.

records.topic: preset maps that tame the bottom (2022)
records.statement: On the 2022, Yamaha's 'Magic Map' preset smoothed the bottom for young aggressive riders while still pulling tall gears; experienced riders preferred the stock map one gear high, and a hill-track map felt tame on a flat track.

source.name: Dirt Bike Test, 2022 Yamaha YZ450F - same bike, new reputation

records.notes: Map names: Magic Map; a tester-made map developed at Glen Helen.

records.statement: The YZ450FX was all-new for 2019 on the 2018 YZ450F's electric-start platform (kick-start removed), took the 2020 YZ450F head and brake updates one year later in 2021, and was redone for 2024 on the 2023 YZ450F platform.

source.name: Dirt Bike Test, 2019 Yamaha YZ450FX riding impression

records.notes: 2021 detail from rx21 and dbt21fx; 2024 from dbt24fx.

records.statement: The 2021 YZ450FX got a lower, compact head, new cams and ports, compression up from 12.8 to 13.0:1, a 1.5 mm longer rod, a steel upper and aluminium lower engine mount (swapped materials), a flexier top clamp, larger front caliper pistons, a 240 mm rear disc (from 245), bars 5 mm lower and Dunlop MX33 tires.

values.front_axle: 1.4 mm smaller inner diameter, about 20% less rigid

source.name: Dirt Bike Test, 2021 Yamaha YZ450FX test

records.notes: Racer X lists the same plus a refined 5-speed and better crankcase breather (rx21). Front-axle direction conflicts with the YZ450F 2020 report; see conflicts.

records.statement: The 2022 and 2023 YZ450FX were minor updates after the 2021 overhaul; the 2022 listed at $9,899.

source.name: Dirt Bike Test, first look 2022 Yamaha four-stroke models

records.notes: Specific 2022 change garbled in source.

records.statement: The 2024 YZ450FX uses the 2023 YZ450F engine and frame with a new wide-ratio tri-shaft 5-speed, off-road ECU maps, three-level traction control in the app, unique clutch friction plates, off-road lower engine mounts and 10 mm shorter suspension; Yamaha claims 251 lb wet, about 3 lb lighter.

source.name: Motocross Action, MXA race test: 2024 Yamaha YZ450FX cross-country

records.notes: Weight claim from dbt24fx.

records.statement: The 2025 YZ450FX changed only graphics.

source.name: Dirt Bike Test, 2025 Yamaha YZ450FX test

records.statement: Yamaha lists for the 2026 YZ450FX an anti-theft ECU lock, four-level traction control in the Power Tuner app, updated switchgear and a hand-adjustable fork compression knob.

source.name: Yamaha Motor USA, 2026 YZ450FX features page

records.notes: Feature page does not mention the 2026 YZ450F's new frame or hydraulic clutch for the FX.

records.statement: Compared with the YZ450F gearbox, the 2024+ FX first gear is like adding 14 teeth to the rear sprocket, second like 6 teeth, third like 1 tooth, fourth like removing half a tooth and fifth like removing 5 teeth.

source.name: Motocross Action, MXA race test: 2024 Yamaha YZ450FX cross-country

records.notes: Tester's sprocket-equivalent comparison, not published ratios.

records.topic: FX vs YZ450F suspension and chassis (2024+)
records.statement: The 2024+ FX uses 4.8 fork springs and a 56 shock spring (YZ450F: 5.0 and 58), forks 10 mm shorter (300 mm travel), a shock with 9 mm less stroke, seat over 10 mm lower, a 2.1 gal tank (YZ: 1.6), 18 in rear wheel, kickstand, skid plate and O-ring chain.

source.name: Motocross Action, MXA race test: 2024 Yamaha YZ450FX cross-country

records.notes: Shrouds 50 mm narrower than the previous FX, pegs 5 mm lower and back.

records.statement: The 2019-2023 FX differs from the YZ450F by its semi-wide gearbox (lower 1st and 2nd, taller 4th and 5th), off-road suspension settings and mapping, a larger tank, 18 in rear wheel, O-ring chain, kickstand, skid plate and different clutch friction plates and lever ratio.

source.name: Dirt Bike Test, 2021 Yamaha YZ450FX test

records.notes: Clutch plates and lever ratio from dbt19fx.

records.statement: The WR450F adds a headlight, taillight, speedometer and cooling fan, a quiet spark-arrestor muffler with a removable restrictor, a steel rear sprocket, softer trail valving and a different ECU, exhaust and flywheel/stator; the FX has none of the lighting and stiffer, MX-oriented suspension.

source.name: Dirt Bike Test, This or that? YZ450FX vs WR450F (2019)

records.notes: Flywheel/stator difference from dbt21fx.

records.statement: On a magazine dyno the 2021 YZ450FX made 53.0 hp at 9,600 rpm and 32.9 lb-ft at 7,100 rpm.

source.name: Dirt Rider, 2021 Yamaha YZ450FX dyno test

records.notes: In-house dyno (same outlet uses a Dynojet 250i); map and fuel not stated; stock. 2022-2023 mechanically similar.

records.statement: The 2019 FX is strong and smooth off the bottom and hard to stall, then lively and free-revving through the mid and top; map 2 is an internal softer setting with a traction-control-like feel.

source.name: Dirt Bike Test, 2019 Yamaha YZ450FX riding impression

records.notes: Test bike's idle was set too low.

records.statement: The 2021-2023 FX makes smooth torque down low and lugs deep without much clutch, builds a little slower than a KTM with no big surges; stock map 1 felt too aggressive and jerky off the bottom.

source.name: Dirt Bike Test, 2021 Yamaha YZ450FX test

records.notes: Testers say it stalls less than rivals.

records.statement: The 2024-2025 FX has crisp, sometimes unsettling low-rpm response, a robust midrange into the top end and about 500 rpm more rev range; it lugs without stalling, first gear is so low it is rarely used and third is the key gear.

source.name: Dirt Bike Test, 2024 Yamaha YZ450FX test

records.notes: Rev-range note and 'almost unusable' first gear from mxa24fx.

records.statement: Testers called the 2019-2020 FX plush and stable, the 2021-2023 more agile and precise but with longer, heavier steering in tight trees, and the 2024+ much lighter-feeling and more precise with a little front squirm under hard braking and less bump compliance.

source.name: Dirt Bike Test, 2024 Yamaha YZ450FX test

records.notes: 2021 comparison from dbt21fx.

records.statement: For a sprint enduro on the 2019 FX, testers took a little fork compression out, added a little shock high-speed compression and kept rear ride height from sitting too low; one tooth smaller rear sprocket helps in tight going.

source.name: Dirt Bike Test, 2019 Yamaha YZ450FX riding impression

records.statement: On the 2021 FX testers ran about 105 mm sag, heavier riders added compression or springs, stock 13/50 gearing suited most terrain with a 48 for desert, and the 2.2 gal tank gave about 50 miles.

source.name: Dirt Bike Test, 2021 Yamaha YZ450FX test

records.statement: For fast GP and desert on the 2024-2025 FX, testers ran 100 mm sag, forks at 5 mm (stock 8) with fork compression 10 out, or 3 mm with the softer engine-mount mod plus 2-3 clicks more compression and 1-2 slower rebound; gearing 14/52 for light riders and 14/53 for heavy riders.

source.name: Dirt Bike Test, 2024-2025 YZ450FX chassis setup tips

records.notes: Shock shortened 3 mm internally (about 10 mm less wheel travel). Maps all zeros. Steering damper fitted. A race test fixed slight head-shake in chop with 2 clicks more fork compression (mxa24fx).

records.topic: FX app power slider in tight terrain
records.statement: In tight terrain testers set the app's 1-5 power slider to 2 on map 1 and 3 on map 2; faster riders kept the all-zero stock map.

source.name: Dirt Bike Test, 2025 Yamaha YZ450FX test

records.notes: Veteran riders preferred a tester-made map (JL GH).

records.statement: FX testers complain of no stock handguards, harsh grips, a cable clutch, a domed filter that still passes dirt, and on the 2019 a clutch that loses bite on sudden release; a 2024 kill/map switch failed after a crash.

source.name: Motocross Action, MXA race test: 2024 Yamaha YZ450FX cross-country

records.notes: 2019 clutch bite and low idle from dbt19fx; switch failure from dbt24fx.

records.statement: The WR450F was redone for 2019 on the 2018 YZ450F platform, updated for 2021 with the 2020 YZ450F head, piston, rod and brakes, carried over for 2022-2023, then all-new for 2024 on the 2023 YZ450F platform with only seat, graphics and ECU-lock changes for 2025-2026.

source.name: Dirt Rider, 2021 Yamaha enduro motorcycles revealed

records.notes: 2022 carryover from dr22en; 2024 from dbt24wr; 2025 from e21_25; 2026 from cap26.

records.statement: The 2021 WR450F got a compact head with steeper valve angles, a higher-compression piston (13.0:1), longer rod, refined wide-ratio 5-speed, revised frame flex, mounts, top clamp and axle, new front caliper, disc and pads, and a new LCD meter with fuel consumption and low-fuel light; $9,799.

source.name: Dirt Rider, 2021 Yamaha enduro motorcycles revealed

records.notes: Compression from um21wr. 2022: no mechanical change, USD 9,899 (dr22en).

records.statement: The 2024 WR450F gets 39 mm intake valves, a new piston and rod, a tri-shaft wide-ratio 5-speed, a model-specific ECU, three-level traction control, KYB springs both ends 10 mm lower with hand-adjustable fork compression, a 2.0 gal tank (down 0.2), lithium battery and 18 in rear wheel; $10,199.

source.name: Dirt Bike Test, first look: all-new 2024 Yamaha WR450F

records.notes: Weight and battery from mcom24wr. Australian spec: 117 kg wet, 2 kg lighter, 7.4 L (mcn24wr).

records.statement: The 2025 WR450F added the motocross models' seamless seat and new graphics; 2026 adds a blue gripper seat, graphics and the Power Tuner ECU lock.

source.name: Enduro21, first look 2025 Yamaha WR range

records.notes: 2026 from a dealer page (cap26).

records.statement: The US WR450F keeps a throttle stop and an inner exhaust baffle, has a locked, encrypted ECU with no Power Tuner access unless the GYTR communication unit is added, but has no air pump, charcoal canister or O2 sensor.

source.name: Dirt Bike, riding the 2021 Yamaha WR450F - the wrap

records.notes: A last-minute evaporative-emissions rule (charcoal canister) cost the 2019 its California green sticker; it is a red-sticker bike (dbtfxwr; um21wr says Yamaha dropped green-sticker compliance for performance).

records.statement: Testers' uncorking steps for the WR450F: remove the throttle stop, remove the airbox intake restrictor, remove the small muffler restrictor or fit an aftermarket exhaust, and install the GYTR competition ECU; together they make the engine package nearly the same as the YZ450FX.

values.steps: throttle stop, airbox restrictor, muffler restrictor/exhaust, GYTR comp ECU

source.name: Dirt Bike Test, This or that? YZ450FX vs WR450F (2019)

records.notes: Closed-course use only. ECU kit parts covered in ypt-058/059/060/061.

records.statement: With the GYTR competition ECU (YZ450FX-equivalent mapping) and a slip-on, testers say the WR gains almost 20 horsepower and runs better than the FX, with a smoother low-end transition.

source.name: Dirt Bike, riding the 2021 Yamaha WR450F - the wrap

records.notes: Tester statement; no dyno sheet published. Consistent with a restricted 2021 WR at 48.9 hp vs an FX at 53.0 hp only if the stock WR test was restricted; see conflicts.

records.statement: On a magazine dyno the 2021 WR450F made 48.9 hp at 9,000 rpm and 31.8 lb-ft at 7,200 rpm.

source.name: Dirt Rider, 2021 Yamaha WR450F dyno test

records.notes: In-house dyno, Dunlop D404 street tire; article describes the EPA-compliant muffler and ECU, so likely in US-restricted form but not stated.

records.statement: The stock 2021 WR450F is docile and torquey to about 5,000 rpm, pulls hard above that with more than a 250 but no 450 hit, tapers near 8,000 and holds to the 11,000 rpm redline; it is great on slow, tight trails and struggles in sand, hills and open terrain.

source.name: Ultimate Motorcycling, 2021 Yamaha WR450F review

records.notes: Sand/hill struggle and tight-trail strength from db21wr.

records.statement: Stock 2021 WR450Fs can stumble, cough and sometimes die when leaned over at low rpm; mapping through the GYTR communication unit cured it even with the stock quiet pipe.

source.name: Dirt Bike, riding the 2021 Yamaha WR450F - the wrap

records.notes: Another 2021 test reported no stalling (um21wr). Older (2017) WR long-term tests also cured climb stalls with a map change and auto clutch.

records.statement: An Australian-spec 2019 WR450F felt strong in deep sand but too aggressive and tiring on hardpack and rocks; the softer handlebar map did not calm it enough, while app maps made it far less aggressive in tight terrain.

source.name: Australasian Dirt Bike, Yamaha WR450F GYTR review (MY19)

records.notes: Australian bikes come with the CCU in a free competition kit.

records.statement: Testers find the 2024 WR450F punchy from mid to top with better low-speed traction; the app can dial it back to roughly 250-like output for beginners, and one tester said it rides like a 350 enduro.

source.name: MCNews (Australia), 2024 Yamaha WR450F review

records.notes: A UK tester estimated about 45 bhp (no dyno) and wanted a sixth gear (mcnuk24wr).

records.statement: WR450F suspension uses the same KYB hardware as the FX with softer trail valving, soft early in the stroke and progressive deeper; the 2024's stock settings felt firm and testers softened them with the new fork compression knobs.

source.name: Dirt Bike Test, This or that? YZ450FX vs WR450F (2019)

records.notes: 2024 firmness from mcn24wr and mcnuk24wr. Firm up for fast desert (um21wr).

records.statement: The 2024 WR450F's clutch pull felt heavy at first; moving the lever perch outward on the bar gave better leverage and a lighter pull.

source.name: MCNews (Australia), 2024 Yamaha WR450F review

records.notes: Single tester.

records.statement: With the GYTR competition ECU fitted, a long press of the kill button after shutdown puts it into sleep mode, turning off the taillight, odometer and map-switch light.

source.name: Dirt Bike Test, first ride 2023 Yamaha WR450F

records.statement: Range claims of up to 80 miles from the 2023 WR450F's tank need very gentle throttle; in sand it ran dry at 35 miles. An Australian tester estimated 80-90 km from the 2024's 7.4 L.

source.name: Dirt Bike Test, first ride 2023 Yamaha WR450F

records.notes: 2024 estimate from mcn24wr.

records.statement: Yamaha Australia recalled WR450F (2016-2020) and WR250F (2018-2019) bikes because the noise label showed the wrong decibel level; dealers replace the label free.

source.name: Yamaha Motor Australia customer notification: WR250F/WR450F noise label

records.notes: Unit count from the government recall listing (accc). Australia only; no US recall found.

records.statement: The WR250F was all-new for 2020 on the YZ250F platform, cosmetic for 2021, updated for 2022 (cams, intake port, shift cam, frame, 270 mm disc, cockpit parts), then all-new again for 2025 with only seat, graphics and ECU-lock changes for 2026.

source.name: Dirt Rider, 2022 Yamaha enduro motorcycles first look

records.notes: 2021 from dr21en; 2025 from e21_25 and up25wr2; 2026 from cap26.

records.statement: The 2020 WR250F got a high-compression forged piston (13.8:1), revised valve angle, exhaust cam timing and balance factor, a lighter clutch with lighter pull, a lighter starter (one-way clutch load cut about 60%), a 350 g lighter shock, a 7.9 L tank and a two-map bar switch; Yamaha Australia claims 115 kg wet, 3 kg less.

source.name: MCNews (Australia), Yamaha WR250F all new for 2020

records.notes: Australian-market launch coverage.

records.statement: The 2025 WR250F gets the YZ250F's wider cam chain, a rear-breathing airbox, a new frame with tank rail and tension pipe 15 mm lower, 10 mm less fork stroke with a compression knob, a 22 mm rear axle, 50 mm slimmer shrouds, a 2.0 gal tank, lithium battery and four-level traction control in the app.

source.name: Enduro21, first look 2025 Yamaha WR range

records.notes: Weights from mcn25wr2 (AU, 2 kg lighter) and up25wr2 (US).

records.statement: On a Dynojet 250i the 2021 WR250F made 36.1 hp at 12,000 rpm and 17.9 lb-ft at 8,100 rpm, 2.9 hp and 0.1 lb-ft less than the YZ250F.

source.name: Dirt Rider, 2021 Yamaha WR250F dyno test

records.notes: Dynojet 250i rear-wheel; restriction state not stated (bike described with USFS spark arrestor, red-sticker eligible, not green-sticker).

records.statement: Owners uncork the US WR250F by removing the security-Torx throttle stop screw and plugging the hole with a short 5 mm bolt, drilling two rivets to remove the muffler restrictor, and snapping off the white intake restrictor behind the backfire screen; removing the tail pipe or spark arrestor runs it lean and should be paired with the competition ECU and about +2 fuel.

values.lean_risk: start +2 fuel if tail pipe/arrestor removed

source.name: Owner technical site (robrobinette.com), WR250F uncork

records.notes: Owner write-up; the throttle stop limiting opening to about 1/3 and the muffler restrictor are corroborated by a magazine kit test on the earlier generation (dbtkit). No dyno numbers. The 2025 uses a different traction-control ECU and the 2020-2024 competition ECU probably does not fit.

records.statement: The competition ECU made an already-uncorked WR250F run stronger but did not change off-idle response; adding the communication unit allowed a softer map with up to -9 ignition and extra low-rpm fuel for a trail feel.

source.name: Owner technical site (robrobinette.com), WR250F uncork

records.notes: Single owner, no dyno. On the earlier generation a magazine found leaning fuel cut stalling and advancing ignition sharpened response (dbtkit).

records.statement: A 2020 WR250F test went from 13/50 to 13/48 to hold second through slower corners, paired with an aftermarket slip-on and header that sharpened response and saved about 1 kg but cost grip in slick going.

source.name: Transmoto, 2020 WR250F 12 bang-for-buck mods

records.notes: Australian-spec bike.

records.statement: Testers find the 2025 WR250F lively with a bigger midrange kick than before; the second handlebar map is softer, flattens the midrange and adds some traction control. The fork can feel stiff on slow technical trails.

source.name: Enduro21, tested 2025 Yamaha WR250F

records.notes: Fork stiffness from up25wr2. Full custom mapping on the US bike needs the GYTR competition ECU (up25wr2).

records.statement: On the 2025 WR250F hot restarts can take several seconds instead of under one, worse after a stall on a hill.

source.name: Enduro21, tested 2025 Yamaha WR250F

records.notes: Similar slow hot-restart complaint on the 2022 YZ450F (dbt22).

records.statement: UK owners of the 2025 WR250F cannot change maps themselves in the app; a dealer must do it under EU/UK rules.

source.name: Enduro21, tested 2025 Yamaha WR250F

2% per step (2018 and 2021 race tests) vs about 3% per step (ypt-011).
Race test: identical to 2021 except rear wheel; another test: slightly stiffer valving; Dirt Bike first look: updated settings.
conflicts.note: Clicker baselines in the 2022 race test (comp 9 stock) differ from the 2018 stock (8).

conflicts.spread: 2018 race test: twitchy, loose, less stable than KTM; 2022 retrospective: 2018/2019 chassis very stable and adaptable.

conflicts.note: Different dynos and correction; never compare across outlets.
